reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-two home runs projected at age 23 is the headline, and the contact profile makes it believable. His 93.0 mph average exit velocity sits at the 96th percentile, and 50.5% hard-hit rate pairs with an 18.2% strikeout rate that's well below what you'd expect from someone swinging that hard, so the .364 xwOBA isn't an accident of timing. The whole thing hinges on the chase and whiff numbers staying where they are — his 29.7% chase rate is league-average, which means pitchers will keep testing him outside, and if he drifts up there, the bat-to-ball edge that makes the projection work starts to erode. If it holds, you're looking at a .278/.363/.529 season from a 23-year-old third baseman with one of the more complete offensive profiles in the American League, just don't ask him to move around the diamond.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong

His .358 xwOBA and 48.5% hard-hit rate say the raw damage is there; his 11.8% walk rate says he's drawing contact on his own terms. The tension is the 34.1% chase rate and 26.4% strikeout rate, which sit in the bottom fifth of the league — if pitchers can exploit that aggression consistently, the hit tool caps the upside and that .273 projection becomes optimistic. But the speed grades at 29.5 ft/s (96th percentile), and a hitter who barrels the ball at a 12.2% rate and runs like that earns the benefit of the doubt on the contact risk.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA is .303 and the xSLG is .508, and the contact profile is doing real work. Witt's 51.1% hard-hit rate and 92.3 mph average exit velocity explain why those expected numbers hold: he hits the ball hard enough, consistently enough, that the .289 projection AVG actually undersells what the underlying contact quality suggests. The chase rate at 33.3% is the one soft spot, and if pitchers tighten that thread, the walk rate and on-base number both get squeezed. But with 30.0 ft/s sprint speed and the projection carrying 42 stolen bases alongside .364 OBP, the ceiling here isn't about one skill — it's about how many ways this profile beats you at once.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells the story here: 13.2% puts Stewart in elite company for contact quality, and the .474 xSLG backs it up without needing the raw exit velocity to be loud. The gap between that xSLG and a 38.5% hard-hit rate is the profile's central wrinkle — he's barreling balls at a rate that outperforms how often he's genuinely squaring things up, which means the power lives in the shape of contact rather than sheer volume of it. If the 27.0% whiff rate creeps up as pitchers attack him harder, the .262/.335/.476 projection line softens, because the walk rate is ordinary and there's no speed floor to fall back on. At 22, though, this is a legitimate middle-of-the-order bat becoming what the contact quality already says he is.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The contact-and-plate-discipline numbers are where this profile gets complicated. Merrill's xSLG sits at .471 and his hard-hit rate is 46.7%, genuine power from a 23-year-old outfielder, but he's chasing 37.4% of pitches outside the zone and walking just 6.5% of the time, and those two facts are hard to separate from each other. The projection absorbs that tension and lands at a .725 OPS across 663 plate appearances, with 26 home runs and 27 steals giving the counting-stat line real shape even if the on-base side stays thin. He's an everyday player right now; the question is whether the discipline ever tightens, because if it does the .471 xSLG points somewhere considerably better than what the projection currently describes.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the headline: 15% strikeouts across AAA & A+ & A translates to 18.7% at the MLB level, well below where most big-league hitters land, and that's with a .237 ISO in tow. At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report: A 16.7% barrel rate is elite contact quality sitting inside one of the worst chase-and-whiff profiles in baseball. That's the whole tension: Goodman hits the ball as hard as anyone, with a 45.7% hard-hit rate backing the barrel number, but a 40.0% chase rate and 35.4% whiff rate leave him unable to get to enough of it consistently, which is why his xBA sits at .233 while his xSLG is .475. The projection threads the needle, .255/.319/.541 with 42 home runs across a full 577 PA season, and that outcome is entirely plausible if pitchers continue to make mistakes in the zone because the barrel rate has the sample shape of someone who does serious damage when he connects. Everything hinges on whether he can cut even a few points off that chase rate; if he doesn't, the strikeouts eat the counting stats and you're left with a slugger who plays catcher but profiles closer to a platoon bat.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Brown's strikeout output sits at 25.3% and his xERA at 3.56, numbers that say mid-rotation contributor, but a 12.9% walk rate is quietly strangling the profile. What keeps the profile functional is the 16.8% strikeout rate and 28.8 ft/s sprint speed, a hitter who puts the ball in play and can actually run once he does. reports.name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .362 and the xSLG is .473, both well above what his current projection line reflects — and that gap is the whole profile in miniature. Acuña is hitting the ball hard enough to be a genuine offensive force, 12.8% barrels with a 12.2% walk rate, but a 29.9% whiff rate is bleeding the contact quality before it scores. The projection's .769 OPS in 476 plate appearances is the post-ACL Acuña still running below what the Statcast profile says he should be, and the sprint speed at 27.1 ft/s explains why 23 projected stolen bases feels conservative on paper but fragile in practice. If the whiff rate compresses as he gets further from the injury, the underlying contact quality is there to push him back toward the player he was; if it doesn't, you're looking at a high-walk, medium-power outfielder who costs you in the batting average column.

reports.name: Carter Jensen
reports.published_report: The contact numbers are brutal, and that's what makes this profile so uncomfortable to hold. Jensen barrels the ball at 10.7% and exits it at 91.0 mph, but a 29.3% whiff rate and an xBA of .202 mean the hard contact arrives infrequently enough to drag his xwOBA down to .292. He doesn't chase at 24.4%, and he draws walks at 11.0%, so the discipline is genuine; the problem is that when he does swing, he misses too often for those exit velocities to accumulate into a useful average. The projection's .225/.310/.415 line across 594 plate appearances is basically the honest translation of that tension: a catcher who hits 22 home runs but costs you something at the plate every time contact becomes an adventure.

reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The contact skill is loud, but the power is almost nowhere. Durbin's 13.0% strikeout rate sits well above the league median in the good direction, and his 15.8% whiff rate is genuinely hard to run into at any level, but an 83.6 mph average exit velocity and 2.7% barrel rate are the kind of contact quality that makes pitchers comfortable working in the zone against him. His xSLG of .321 says the ball isn't going far when he does make contact, which is why the projected .397 SLG leans so heavily on the 20 stolen bases carrying the offensive floor. He becomes a steady low-end regular if the legs stay under him, and a platoon-limited bench piece the moment the stolen base engine slows.

reports.published_report: The 3.59 ERA projection is doing Weathers a favor, and the Statcast profile explains why. His xERA sits at 4.28 with an xwOBA of .319, both in the bottom third of the league, and hitters are making hard contact at a 40.6% clip — his control is the one thing holding this together. At 6.7% walks with 25.2% strikeouts, the command-to-stuff ratio is genuinely inverted from what you want in a rotation piece: he limits free passes, but he isn't missing bats at a rate that punishes the contact he allows. If the control slips even modestly, there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him, and a starter posting an xERA like that becomes a reliever-by-necessity story pretty quickly.

reports.name: Roki Sasaki
reports.published_report:
The fastball at 97.8 mph is elite. The problem is what happens after it.

Sasaki's 29.7% whiff rate and 33.4% chase rate say he misses bats at a real clip, but the barrel and hard-hit numbers tell a different story: hitters who do make contact are doing damage, with a 10.0% barrel rate and 43.1% hard-hit rate that land in the bottom tier of the league. If it doesn't, a bloated WHIP and loud contact are the outcome, not a stepping stone.

reports.published_report: The xERA of 3.01 and xwOBA of .270 tell a genuinely compelling story, but the mechanism is unusual enough to pause on. Miles gets hitters out by keeping the ball on the ground and off the barrel, a 3.8% barrel rate in the 94th percentile and average exit velocity sitting at 86.8 mph, rather than by missing bats, and his 18.3% whiff rate in the 5th percentile makes that explicit. The 6.0% walk rate is clean, and when hitters do put the ball in play they're not squaring it up, which is how you post results that look like a mid-bullpen strikeout artist without actually being one. If his contact management regresses and the chase rate, already at 28.5%, dips further, there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him, so the profile lives and dies on weak contact, and with 92.7 projected innings and a 3.03 ERA he's priced as a legitimate bullpen contributor for Toronto whose Statcast contact suppression says the number is earned.

Across AA & A+ in 2026, Randall has posted a 3.0 BB/9 over 118.3 innings, which translates to roughly league-average walk territory at the MLB level, but his 9.0 K/9 translates to a 7.5, well short of the 8.6 MLB average, and that gap is what keeps a 1.3 WHIP and a 4.9 ERA from reading as a functional ceiling profile. The 40 walks in 118 innings tell you he can find the zone; the 118 strikeouts tell you hitters aren't afraid of what's in it. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb as he sees better lineups, the command advantage gets neutralized and you're left with a depth arm, which is exactly where both his ceiling and floor land.

reports.name: Ernie Clement
reports.published_report: The contact rate carries the profile and the power undercuts it at every turn. Clement's 9.8% strikeout rate puts him among the rarest company in the league for bat-to-ball, and his 16.1% whiff rate shows the contact isn't incidental — he's genuinely hard to miss. But a 2.2% barrel rate and 84.3 mph average exit velocity scrape the bottom of the Statcast floor, and an xSLG of .329 is the honest shape of what that contact produces. The projection's .279 AVG is believable on the contact profile alone; the .304 OBP tells you the 3.4% walk rate leaves no cushion, and if the soft contact stops finding holes, what remains is a utility piece whose bat grades out as a liability.

If he stays on the field and the strikeout rate stabilizes, the .343 xwOBA is a real foundation; if he can't, you're looking at a good-bat-limited-games second-division regular.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.name: Drew Cavanaugh
reports.published_report: The .449 OBP across AAA & AA is doing a lot of work here, and the BABIP of .401 is doing most of the heavy lifting behind it. Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

reports.name: Yamal Encarnacion
reports.published_report: The stolen bases carry this profile. Forty-eight at AA across 395 plate appearances is a legitimate weapon, and the 18 K% at that level translates to 21.3% in the majors, right at the 22.0% MLB average, meaning the contact ability that makes the speed playable should survive the climb. The power doesn't travel: a .117 ISO at AA becomes .11 in an MLB context, and the average sits at .15. If the legs and bat-to-ball hold, he's a bench bat who can change a game on the bases; if the speed diminishes even a little, what's left is a second baseman without enough thump to force regular playing time.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Michael Morales
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. reports.published_report: The translation is the problem. If the hit tool sharpens and the strikeout rate drops, there's a low-end regular hiding in a left field profile; if it doesn't, 15 walks in 204 plate appearances across AAA & AA is the whole argument, and that's a bench bat at best.

If the walks come down, there's a back-end arm in here somewhere; if they don't, the ceiling is depth.

Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.

reports.published_report: The shoulder is the whole read. Across 44.7 innings at AAA this season, Mena posted a 19% K-BB%, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout and walk rates nearly identical to what a league-average arm produces. If he comes back healthy, the ceiling is a depth arm who eats innings without embarrassing himself; if the right shoulder doesn't hold, what's left is a bullpen lottery ticket on a very thin resume.
